title: Patch day downloads
brief: A popular game ships a 5 GB update at 10 am. Millions of players press Update within the same hour. The files are identical for everyone, so the work is moving huge amounts of data without a huge bill, while players still log in and play.

clarify.q: Is every player downloading the same file?
clarify.a: Yes, for each platform. The same file is requested millions of times.
A bit. Players accept a few minutes. Logging in must stay quick.
A great deal. Moving data out is the largest cost of the day.

notes: The update is about 5 GB, cut into 8 MB pieces (approx.).
Most pieces are asked for by millions of players in one hour (approx.).

numbers.label: Piece requests per second at peak
Data to send in the first hour
numbers.how: About 2.4 million players × 5 GB ≈ 12 PB, which is 12,000 TB (approx.)

numbers.label: Share served from the edge copy
numbers.how: The same pieces are requested by everyone, so a CDN hits almost always (approx.)

hints: Millions ask for the same pieces. What should answer them, and what should never see them?
A CDN with a very long copy time and an origin shield serves each piece from the origin only a few times.
CDN, origin shield, object storage for the pieces; a separate small path of servers for login and profiles.

editorial.summary: The pieces never change, so they are the ideal thing to cache. A CDN with a long time-to-keep serves almost all of them, an origin shield collapses misses into one fetch, and object storage is only touched a few times per piece.

designs.name: Long edge copies and an origin shield
designs.why: The CDN keeps each piece for a week, so it fetches it from the origin once per edge location. The shield collapses those into one trip to object storage. Login and profile calls use a small separate set of servers and are never queued behind downloads.

tradeoffs: A week-long copy time almost removes origin load. It needs versioned file names, so a fixed file is never served stale.
A cheaper bulk CDN tier costs less per terabyte but is slower. Many studios use it for patches.
Letting players share pieces with each other cuts bandwidth further, but adds complexity and trust questions.
Spreading the release over a few hours smooths the peak and the cost.
editorial.realWorld: Big game patches move petabytes in a day. Studios rely on edge networks and often stagger the release by region to keep the peak in check (approx.).
